Chapter.Content: 30 — Depth, projection, and shadow-map precision
Reading map · Previous chapter · Next chapter

Depth buffers encode an ordering decision under finite precision, and projection choices determine where that precision is spent. This chapter connects conventional depth, reverse-Z, and shadow comparisons to geometry and camera range.

Content.Strong: HZB is not the same thing as ordinary early-Z

Chapter.Content: Early-Z occurs while rasterizing fragments.
The triangle is already submitted and rasterization has begun.
HZB object culling attempts to reject geometry before submitting its expensive draw/mesh work.

NVIDIA’s occlusion-culling discussions make the same broad distinction: depth testing can cheaply discard individual hidden fragments, while hierarchical/object-level visibility systems aim to avoid processing whole objects or hierarchy nodes when they are known to be hidden. NVIDIA Developer

Hardware GPUs also maintain internal hierarchical depth representations for efficient depth rejection; application-built HZBs are conceptually related but are not necessarily the same data structure as the hardware’s private Hi-Z metadata. GPUOpen documents hardware Hi-Z metadata being maintained and resummarized as depth data changes. AMD GPUOpen

That is much worse than rendering an unnecessary hidden object.

Content.Strong: The unifying picture of all structures in Pass 08

Chapter.Content: Now compare the central abstraction each structure uses.
The deeper point is:
A hash grid hypothesizes useful locality at one fixed spatial scale.
SAP hypothesizes strong temporal coherence.
KD-tree hypothesizes point-like data and useful axis separation.
Portal/PVS hypothesizes a cell-connected architectural environment.
HZB hypothesizes enough existing screen-space occlusion to make depth rejection worthwhile.
If that hypothesis is false, the data structure can become slower than the simpler alternative.

Content.Strong: Choosing between dynamic tree, SAP and spatial hash

Chapter.Content: Imagine 50,000 particles uniformly spread through a cubic region, all roughly equal size.
Spatial hash is attractive.
Imagine 5,000 rigid bodies moving smoothly with similar frame-to-frame order.
SAP can be very effective.
Imagine 10,000 differently sized rigid bodies moving arbitrarily through a world.
Dynamic AABB tree is more general.
Imagine millions of static reconstructed triangles.

Imagine millions of static point samples requiring nearest-neighbor search.
KD-tree is a stronger candidate.
Imagine an indoor level consisting of rooms and corridors.

A funnel provides useful geometric corners.
It does not solve:
A useful architecture is:
Chapter.Code: A* ↓ polygon corridor ↓ funnel ↓ corner sequence ↓ steering ↓ locomotion / physics
Chapter.Content: Trying to make string pulling itself solve all movement behavior usually produces an overly complicated and brittle layer. This separation is also emphasized by the Recast/Detour author’s practical funnel guidance: graph search selects a corridor, string pulling gives directions through it, and steering/locomotion handles final movement. digestingduck.blogspot.com
The basic funnel algorithm treats the agent as a point.
For an agent with radius , portal clearance must account for that radius.
A common solution is to build/erode the navmesh for a particular agent radius.
Then an agent center can safely be treated as a point moving over the already-clearance-adjusted mesh.
If instead using a generic mesh, portals need to be shrunk by radius and corners offset appropriately.
This becomes complicated around sharp turns.
That is why navigation meshes are usually generated from explicit agent configuration:
Chapter.Code: radius height max slope step height
Chapter.Content: rather than using raw render geometry directly.
A navmesh describes static walkable space well.
But worlds contain:
Chapter.Code: closed doors moving crates vehicles temporary barriers fallen debris crowds
Chapter.Content: There are several levels of dynamic response.
The first is cost modification.
Instead of deleting navigation topology, temporarily increase cost:

Chapter.Content: This works well for discrete dynamic state changes.
Your current generic NavigationGraph does not expose an enabled/disabled edge flag, but such a flag would be straightforward.
For an obstacle occupying part of a nav polygon, merely disabling the entire polygon may be overly conservative.
You can carve the obstacle shape out of walkable space and retriangulate/repolygonize the local region.
This gives accurate navigation but modification is much more expensive.
Therefore dynamic navmesh systems often divide the world into tiles.
Only affected tiles are rebuilt.

Recast/Detour’s tile-cache API follows exactly that model: obstacle changes mark affected tiles, and updates rebuild the touched tiles incrementally rather than regenerating the whole navigation mesh. Recast Navigation

Rebuilding navmesh geometry for every other agent every frame would be absurd.

Chapter.Content: This separates two timescales.
Global pathfinding handles persistent geometry.
Steering handles rapidly changing local interactions.
This is analogous to broadphase/narrowphase separation in collision detection.

Content.Strong: A* repository audit before leaving M083

Chapter.Content: Your generic A* implementation has several strong properties.

It validates finite/nonnegative edge costs, handles start/goal absence cleanly, uses duplicate heap entries instead of requiring decrease-key, skips stale entries, protects against accumulated float overflow, records expansion count, reconstructs through cameFrom, and computes a Euclidean heuristic scale that remains safe when edge costs are cheaper than geometric distance.
There are also improvements available.

The generic priority queue has no deterministic secondary tie-breaker, so equal- routes may not have fully deterministic expansion ordering. Computing the global heuristic scale scans every edge on every path query, which can become expensive; because graph topology/costs usually change much less frequently than queries, the scale could be cached and invalidated when edges change. unordered_map storage is flexible but expensive for dense contiguous navigation IDs; vector-backed arrays can be much faster when node indices are compact.
The navmesh pathfinder has excellent deterministic tie-breaking by , then , then polygon ID, but as discussed, discounted AreaCost < 1 can invalidate its unscaled Euclidean heuristic.
